Growing Greenhouse Tomatoes

Greenhouse tomatoes reward planning: pick the right variety, water on a schedule, feed the fruit rather than the vine, and scout for pests weekly. This guide walks through a full season under glass.

Choosing Varieties

Indeterminate varieties earn their keep in a greenhouse because the vines crop continuously. San Marzano remains the paste benchmark and shrugs off cracking. For slicing, the heirloom Brandywine delivers the best flavor of anything we trialed, though yields trail modern hybrids by a third.

Watering

Drip irrigation beats overhead watering under glass: foliage stays dry and fungal pressure drops sharply. Mature plants need about 2.5 litres per plant daily at fruit set, delivered in two pulses. Mulch the root zone with straw to even out the swings between pulses.

Nutrients

Blossom end rot is a calcium transport problem, not a soil deficiency: irregular watering blocks calcium from reaching the fruit. Fix the schedule first, then apply a calcium nitrate foliar spray weekly until new fruit sets clean. Switch to a low-nitrogen, high-potassium feed once trusses form.

Pests

The tomato hornworm does the fastest damage: a single larva strips a truss overnight. Scout the undersides of leaves at dusk and hand-pick. Companion planting basil between rows measurably reduces whitefly settling, and the basil crop pays for the bench space.

Harvest

Pick at the breaker stage, when the blossom end first blushes: the fruit ripens indoors with no loss of flavor and the vine redirects energy to the next truss. Most greenhouse varieties run 65 to 80 days from transplant to first harvest.
